title: Potiphar's house (Genesis 39)
hook: a slave, falsely accused, and yet the Lord was with Joseph

segments.voice: Yesterday, bor: a dry cistern, twenty pieces of silver, and a coat dipped in goat's blood. Your line was the pit is not the end. Who did you hold in mind? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

Some people end up in a job they never chose. A night shift taken because the rent was due. A family business you were drafted into. A first job in a city where you know no one, doing work far below what you hoped for. Now take that and make it far worse. Joseph is barely more than a boy, in a foreign country, and he has been sold. He is a slave in the house of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard. Nobody from home knows where he is. His father thinks he's dead. And the chapter's first line about him is not what you'd expect.
screen: `A JOB YOU NEVER CHOSE.` → `SOLD, SEVENTEEN, ALONE.` → `POTIPHAR'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian." Notice the order. The Lord was with him, and he was still in his master's house. Being with God did not mean getting out. It meant that, where he was, things went well. Potiphar notices, and puts him in charge of everything he owns. Then Potiphar's wife notices him too. Joseph is handsome, the text says, and day after day she presses him to sleep with her. He refuses, and gives his reason: his master has trusted him with everything, "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" One day, when the house is empty, she grabs him by his garment. He runs, and leaves it in her hand. Count the garments: his coat was stripped off by his brothers, and now another is left in his master's wife's hand. And again the clothing is used to tell a lie. She tells the household, and then her husband, that Joseph attacked her. Potiphar is furious, and Joseph is thrown into prison. He did the right thing and lost everything again. And then the chapter repeats itself, almost word for word: "But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy." The keeper of the prison puts him in charge of the other prisoners. Twice in one chapter, from the top of a house to the bottom of a prison, the same line. Some readers hold onto this chapter for that reason. It doesn't promise Joseph safety. It says, twice, that he wasn't alone where he landed.
screen: `WITH HIM, AND STILL A SLAVE.` · `HOW CAN I SIN AGAINST GOD?` · `ANOTHER GARMENT, ANOTHER LIE.` · `IN PRISON, THE SAME LINE.` · then, large: `THE LORD WAS WITH JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do good work where you're stuck. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place in your life you'd leave if you could: a job, a role, a situation that isn't fair. Picture yourself there tomorrow. Now find one small piece of it you could do well anyway, with care, not for anyone's praise. Picture doing it. If you pray, you can ask God to be with you there. If you don't, simply notice that you can bring something good into a place you didn't choose. The bell holds the time.
Potiphar's house. Where Joseph served as a slave, rose to run everything, refused his master's wife, and was falsely accused.
Your line: the lord was with him. Today, in the part of your day you'd most like to skip, do one task as well as you can. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Christians turn to Genesis 39 in seasons of unfair treatment or unwanted work, and the repeated line "the LORD was with Joseph" is often used in sermons and devotions about God's presence in hard places.

original.note: Hebrew: prospering, making things succeed. Genesis uses this root for Joseph in Potiphar's house and in prison.

trapdoor: what you thought: God was with Joseph, so things went his way.
what it means: God was with him as a slave and as a prisoner. the line doesn't promise escape; it promises company.
what a scholar hears: the chapter is framed by the same phrase near its start and end (verses 2–3 and 21–23), so the reader hears God's presence in both the house and the prison.
